front: Alternating voltage and alternating current
back: The electric mains supply is a voltage that varies like a sine function with time - an alternating voltage (ac voltage). The current it drives in a circuit is an alternating current (ac current). 'Ac' is used throughout for a quantity with simple harmonic time dependence, even though 'ac voltage' is strictly redundant.

front: Why ac is used for transmission
back: Ac voltage can be easily and efficiently changed from one value to another by a transformer, so electrical energy can be transmitted economically over long distances. Ac circuits also have properties exploited in everyday devices - tuning a radio to a station uses resonance.

front: ac voltage applied to a resistor
back: v = v_m sin(omega t) gives i = i_m sin(omega t) with i_m = v_m/R. Voltage and current are in phase and reach zero, minimum and maximum together, so V = I R holds for rms values - Ohm's law works for ac as for dc.

front: Why the average ac current is zero but the average power is not
back: Positive and negative values of the current cancel over a full cycle, so the mean current is zero. But Joule heating is i^2 R and i^2 is positive in both half cycles, so energy is dissipated throughout: the average power is (1/2) i_m^2 R, not zero.

front: rms (effective) current and voltage
back: I = sqrt(<i^2>) = i_m/sqrt(2) = 0.707 i_m and V = v_m/sqrt(2) = 0.707 v_m. The rms current is the dc current that would produce the same average power loss. With rms values, P = I^2 R = V I and V = I R, exactly as for dc.

front: Mains 220 V - rms or peak?
back: The value quoted for an ac supply is always the rms value, so 220 V rms corresponds to a peak of v_m = sqrt(2) x 220 = 311 V. Use rms with rms and peak with peak; never mix them in one equation.

front: Phasor (definition)
back: A phasor is a vector rotating about the origin with angular speed omega. Its magnitude is the amplitude (v_m or i_m) of the oscillating quantity and its vertical component is the instantaneous value v or i. A phasor diagram therefore shows both amplitudes and relative phases.

front: Phasors are not vectors
back: Voltage and current in an ac circuit are scalars. Rotating vectors are used only because the amplitudes and phases of harmonically varying scalars combine mathematically like the projections of rotating vectors, so ordinary vector addition may be used.

front: ac voltage applied to an inductor
back: From v - L di/dt = 0, i = i_m sin(omega t - pi/2) with i_m = v_m/X_L. The current lags the voltage by pi/2 - one quarter of a period - and the inductive reactance X_L = omega L = 2 pi nu L rises with frequency.

front: Average power in a pure inductor
back: p_L = i v = -i_m v_m sin(2 omega t)/2, whose average over a full cycle is zero. Energy is stored in the magnetic field and returned to the source, never dissipated - the current is wattless.

front: ac voltage applied to a capacitor
back: With v = q/C and i = dq/dt, i = i_m sin(omega t + pi/2) with i_m = v_m/X_C. The current leads the voltage by pi/2, and the capacitive reactance X_C = 1/(omega C) = 1/(2 pi nu C) falls with frequency and with capacitance.

front: Capacitor on dc versus on ac
back: On dc the capacitor charges and then blocks the current, so a series lamp stays dark and nothing changes if C is reduced. On ac it charges and discharges every half cycle, so charge keeps flowing and the lamp glows; a smaller C means a larger reactance and a dimmer lamp.

front: Series LCR circuit - loop equation
back: L di/dt + i R + q/C = v, with the same current i = i_m sin(omega t + phi) in all three elements at every instant, where phi is the phase difference between the source voltage and the current.

front: Impedance of a series LCR circuit
back: Z = sqrt(R^2 + (X_C - X_L)^2), with i_m = v_m/Z. V is the hypotenuse of a right triangle with sides V_R and (V_C + V_L); dividing by i_m turns that triangle into the impedance triangle.

front: Phase angle and the nature of the circuit
back: tan phi = (X_C - X_L)/R. If X_C > X_L, phi > 0: the circuit is capacitive and the current leads the source voltage. If X_C < X_L, phi < 0: the circuit is inductive and the current lags.

front: Steady state versus transient solution
back: The phasor diagram fixes only the relative angles, so it gives the steady-state solution, not the general solution. A transient solution also exists (even for v = 0); the general solution is the sum of the two, and after a sufficiently long time the transient dies out.

front: Resonance and resonant frequency
back: Resonance is the large response of a system driven near its natural frequency. In a series LCR circuit X_C = X_L at omega_0 = 1/sqrt(LC), so Z = sqrt(R^2 + 0) = R is a minimum and the current amplitude i_m = v_m/R is a maximum.

front: Resonance needs both L and C
back: Only when both L and C are present do their voltages (pi out of phase) cancel at omega_0, leaving the whole source voltage across R. There is no resonance in a pure RL or pure RC circuit.

front: Tuning a radio by resonance
back: The antenna picks up signals from many stations. Varying the capacitance of the tuning circuit makes its resonant frequency nearly equal to that of the wanted signal, whose current amplitude then becomes maximum.

front: Quality factor of a series RLC circuit
back: Q = omega_0 L / R = 1/(omega_0 C R). It is dimensionless and measures how sharp the resonance is relative to the resistance of the circuit.

front: Average power and the power factor
back: p = v i gives P = (v_m i_m/2) cos phi = V I cos phi = I^2 Z cos phi = I^2 R. The quantity cos phi (= R/Z) is the power factor: power dissipated depends on the phase angle as well as on V and I.

front: Wattless current and power-factor correction
back: In a pure L or pure C, phi = pi/2, cos phi = 0 and no power is dissipated - the current is wattless. A lagging wattless component I_q can be cancelled by connecting a capacitor of suitable value in parallel, whose leading I_q' makes Z tend to R and cos phi tend to 1.

front: Transformer - principle and turns ratio
back: Two insulated coils on a soft-iron core, linked by mutual induction: v_s/v_p = N_s/N_p. With negligible losses i_p v_p = i_s v_s, so i_p/i_s = v_s/v_p = N_s/N_p. A step-up transformer has N_s > N_p (V_s > V_p, I_s < I_p); a step-down one has N_s < N_p.

front: Transformer equations - assumptions
back: (i) primary resistance and current small, (ii) the same flux links both windings because little flux escapes the core, (iii) the secondary current is small. Then v_s/v_p = N_s/N_p and, for 100 percent efficiency, i_p v_p = i_s v_s.

front: Energy losses in a real transformer
back: Flux leakage - wind the coils one over the other. Resistance of the windings (I^2 R heating) - use thick wire. Eddy currents in the core - use a laminated core. Hysteresis from repeated magnetisation - use a low-hysteresis magnetic material. A good transformer is still over 95 percent efficient.

front: Free oscillations of an LC circuit
back: A charged capacitor connected across an inductor forms a loop in which the charge oscillates at omega = 1/sqrt(LC) - the same frequency at which a series LCR circuit resonates. Energy alternates between the electric field of the capacitor and the magnetic field of the inductor.
